name: Michigan

agency.name: Michigan Department of State (Secretary of State)

knowledgeTest.roadSigns: The Secretary of State knowledge test for new drivers 18 and older has two parts that must both be passed: an "Operator" multiple-choice section (about 45 minutes) and a separate "Signs" section (about 15 minutes). The number of questions in each part is not published.
knowledgeTest.format: Teens under 18: the Driver Education Segment 1 state exam, an 80-question written test generated for each student by the Michigan Department of State, given by the certified driver education provider (70% to pass). Adults 18+: a multiple-choice computer test plus a road sign test at a Secretary of State office (scheduled up to one hour before closing, no fee) or online at home with webcam identity checks ($6.50 convenience fee).
knowledgeTest.languages: The Secretary of State test is available in English and a number of foreign languages, in audio and written formats; foreign-language interpreters may be used on all written tests except CDL knowledge tests. The handbook is published in English, Spanish, Arabic, Chinese, Dari, French, Pashto, Swahili and Vietnamese.
knowledgeTest.retestWait: Adult SOS test: failing ends the session and you must reschedule for a different day; the online test may be taken up to two times per calendar day (fee each time). Teen Segment 1/2 exams: a student who scores below 70% may retake the test up to two times, using a different version.
knowledgeTest.notes: Michigan teens do not take a separate Secretary of State knowledge test: they must score at least 70% on the Segment 1 state exam (80 questions per the MDOS Driver Education Curriculum Guide) before applying for a Level 1 Learner's License at 14 years, 9 months, and 70% on the 20-question Segment 2 exam. Adults 18+ who have never been licensed take the SOS knowledge and road sign tests (the number of questions and passing score are not published) to get a temporary instruction permit (TIP), valid 180 days; passed test results are valid for one year. Drivers from another U.S. state, Canada, Germany or South Korea can convert their license without a knowledge test.

cdlTest.notes: All CDL knowledge tests require at least 80%. Group A: 70 questions plus a 20-question combination vehicle test; Groups B and C: 50 questions on each test; T, P, S and N endorsements: 20 questions each; H (hazardous materials): 30 questions; air brakes: 25 questions. Only one test per day per testing category.

facts.detail: Michigan's operating-while-intoxicated (OWI) law makes it illegal to drive with an alcohol content of 0.08 or more. You can also be charged if you are under the influence of alcohol or drugs at any BAC.

source.quote: (b) The person has an alcohol content of 0.08 grams or more per 100 milliliters of blood, per 210 liters of breath, or per 67 milliliters of urine

facts.value: 0.02% BAC, or any alcohol from drinking (zero tolerance)
facts.detail: Drivers under 21 may not drive with any bodily alcohol content: 0.02 or more (but under 0.08), or any alcohol in the body from drinking other than as part of a religious ceremony. The handbook lists 4 points for a driver younger than 21 with any bodily alcohol content.

source.quote: A person who is less than 21 years of age, whether licensed or not, shall not operate a vehicle on a highway or other place open to the general public or generally accessible to motor vehicles, including an area designated for the parking of vehicles, within this state if the person has any bodily alcohol content. As used in this subsection, "any bodily alcohol content" means either of the following: (a) An alcohol content of 0.02 grams or more but less than 0.08 grams per 100 milliliters of blood

facts.detail: A person may not operate a commercial motor vehicle with an alcohol content of 0.04 or more.

source.quote: A person, whether licensed or not, who has an alcohol content of 0.04 grams or more but less than 0.08 grams per 100 milliliters of blood, per 210 liters of breath, or per 67 milliliters of urine

facts.value: 1-year license suspension for a first refusal
facts.detail: By applying for or renewing a license, Michigan drivers are considered to have consented to a chemical test. A first refusal (non-commercial vehicle) brings a 1-year suspension; a second refusal within 7 years brings 2 years. The handbook also lists refusal as a 6-point violation.

source.quote: If the person was operating a vehicle other than a commercial motor vehicle, suspend or deny the person's operator's or chauffeur's license or permit to drive, or nonresident operating privilege, for 1 year or, for a second or subsequent refusal within 7 years, for 2 years.

facts.value: Up to 93 days in jail, up to $500 fine, license suspension, 6 points
facts.detail: The handbook says penalties for operating under the influence (alcohol or marijuana) can include up to 93 days in jail, up to a $500 fine, license suspension and six points, with heightened penalties if minors are in the vehicle. By statute (MCL 257.319), a first OWI conviction brings a 180-day suspension with no restricted license for the first 30 days.

source.quote: The penalties for operating under the influence of marijuana are the same as operating under the influence of alcohol. These penalties can include up to 93 days in jail, up to a $500 fine, license suspension, six points on a person's driving record, and more.

facts.value: No open or unsealed alcohol in the passenger area
facts.detail: A driver or passenger may not transport or possess alcohol in an open, uncapped or unsealed container in the passenger area of a vehicle on a highway. The handbook lists an open alcohol container as a 2-point violation.

source.quote: a person who is an operator or occupant shall not transport or possess alcoholic liquor in a container that is open or uncapped or upon which the seal is broken within the passenger area of a vehicle upon a highway

facts.value: 14 years, 9 months (Level 1 Learner's License)
facts.detail: Teens can start driver education Segment 1 at 14 years, 8 months, and apply for the GDL Level 1 Learner's License at 14 years, 9 months, with a parent or guardian and a Segment 1 certificate.

source.quote: GDL Level 1 Learner's License: To apply, you must be at least 14 years, 9 months old, visit a Secretary of State office with your parent or legal guardian, pass the vision and health standards

facts.value: 6 months (Level 1)
facts.detail: You must hold the Level 1 Learner's License for at least six months before you can get the Level 2 Intermediate License (and at least three months before starting Segment 2).

source.quote: GDL Level 2 Intermediate License: To apply, you must be at least age 16 and have held your Level 1 Learner's License for at least 6 months.

facts.value: 50 hours, including 10 at night
facts.detail: Level 1 teens must log at least 50 hours of supervised driving, including 10 hours at night, before the driving skills test. At least 30 hours (2 at night) must be logged before starting Segment 2.

source.quote: You must keep a driving log that tracks your supervised driving time (and complete a minimum of 50 hours, including 10 hours at night) before taking the driving skills test.

facts.value: Licensed parent/guardian or designated licensed adult 21+ in the front seat
facts.detail: A Level 1 driver may drive only with a licensed parent, guardian or designated licensed adult age 21 or older seated in the front seat next to them. A designated adult needs a signed letter of authorization from the parent or guardian.

source.quote: Once the Level 1 Learner's License is issued, you may only drive with a licensed parent, guardian or designated, licensed adult age 21 or older seated in the front seat next to you.

facts.value: 16 (Level 2 Intermediate License)
facts.detail: The Level 2 Intermediate License requires age 16, at least 6 months with the Level 1 license, and no violations, at-fault crashes or suspensions in the 90 days before applying.

source.quote: GDL Level 2 Intermediate License: To apply, you must be at least age 16 and have held your Level 1 Learner's License for at least 6 months.

facts.value: No driving 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. (Level 2)
facts.detail: Level 2 drivers may not drive between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. unless accompanied by a parent, guardian or designated licensed adult 21+, or driving for work or to/from work or an authorized activity.

source.quote: Level 2 Intermediate License restrictions prohibit you from driving between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. unless one of the following applies

facts.value: No more than 1 passenger under 21 (Level 2)
facts.detail: Level 2 drivers may not carry more than one passenger under 21 unless a parent, guardian or designated adult 21+ is in the vehicle, the passengers are immediate family, or the trip is for work or an authorized activity.

source.quote: You may not have more than one passenger under the age of 21 in the vehicle with you at any time unless one of the following applies

facts.value: 17 (Level 3 Full License)
facts.detail: Level 3 requires age 17, at least six months at Level 2, and 12 consecutive months without a moving violation, at-fault crash, suspension or GDL violation. It is issued automatically at no fee. GDL ends at 18.

source.quote: GDL Level 3 Full License: To be eligible, you must be at least age 17 and have held the Level 2 Intermediate License for at least six months.

facts.value: Hand-held device use banned for all drivers
facts.detail: Michigan's cell phone law (MCL 257.602b) bans holding or using a mobile electronic device while driving, including calls, texts, videos and social media. Hands-free use with a single touch or swipe is allowed for drivers who are not Level 1 or 2 teens.

source.quote: Michigan's general cell phone law (MCL 257.602b) prohibits all drivers from using a cell phone while driving. This means you cannot hold or use a mobile electronic device, such as a cell phone or tablet, while operating a motor vehicle on a public road, street, highway, or other public venue.

facts.value: Texting banned; $100 first offense, $250 after
facts.detail: Hand-held use, including reading or sending texts, is illegal. Fines are $100 for a first offense and $250 for later violations; exceptions exist for reporting crashes, crimes or other emergencies.

source.quote: Using a hand-held phone while driving is illegal in Michigan and this includes reading, texting, or making or answering a call. Exceptions are in place for reporting crashes, crimes or other emergencies. Drivers face a fine of $100 for a first offense and $250 for subsequent violations.

facts.value: Kelsey's Law: Level 1 and 2 drivers may not use a phone (even hands-free) except in emergencies
facts.detail: Kelsey's Law (MCL 257.602c) bars teens with a GDL Level 1 or Level 2 license from making or receiving non-emergency phone calls while driving; violators could face a civil infraction with fines and/or community service.

source.quote: Non-emergency exceptions: Kelsey's Law (MCL 257.602c) prohibits teens with a GDL 1 or GDL 2 from making or receiving non-emergency phone calls.

facts.value: Driver and front-seat passengers; everyone under 16 in all seats
facts.detail: All front-seat occupants (including the driver) must be buckled, and all passengers under 16 must be buckled in every seating position. An officer may stop a vehicle if occupants are not properly buckled.

source.quote: All front seat passengers to be buckled up (including the driver).

facts.value: Car seat or booster until age 8 or 4'9" tall
facts.detail: Children must ride in a car seat or booster until they are 8 years old or 4 feet 9 inches tall, whichever comes first. Children under 4 must ride in a rear seat if the vehicle has one (unless all rear seats are taken by children under 4).

source.quote: Children are to be properly buckled up in a car seat or booster seat until they are 8 years old or 4 feet 9 inches tall.

facts.value: Careful and prudent speed; able to stop within the clear distance ahead
facts.detail: Drive at a careful and prudent speed for conditions that always lets you stop within the clear distance ahead. That speed is never faster than the posted limit and may be slower.

source.quote: Michigan's Basic Speed Law means you must drive at a "careful and prudent" speed in all driving conditions. Drive at a speed that always allows you to stop within the clear distance ahead.

facts.value: As posted (at least 25 mph; up to 20 mph below the normal limit)
facts.detail: The handbook says school-zone limits vary and must be watched for. By statute, a school-zone limit may be up to 20 mph below the normal limit but not less than 25 mph, and applies around the start and end of the school day (generally up to 30 minutes before and after).

source.quote: may be decreased by not more than 20 miles per hour less than the speed limit normally posted but shall be not less than 25 miles per hour

facts.value: 25 mph (platted subdivisions and condominium complexes)
facts.detail: The standard limit in platted subdivisions and condominium complexes is 25 mph. Mobile home parks and some municipal parks are 15 mph.

source.quote: 25 mph – In platted subdivisions (showing boundaries, streets, easements and other features of surveyed lots) and condominium complexes.

facts.value: 25 mph
facts.detail: Unless otherwise posted, the speed limit on a highway segment within a business district is 25 mph. The handbook advises watching for posted limits in business districts.

source.quote: Twenty-five miles per hour on a highway segment within a business district.

facts.value: 55 mph
facts.detail: Unless otherwise posted, the limit is 55 mph on all highways and streets that are not freeways.

source.quote: 55 mph – Unless otherwise posted, on all streets that are not designated freeways and on all highways.

facts.value: 70 mph (unless posted otherwise)
facts.detail: Freeways have a 70 mph maximum and 55 mph minimum unless posted otherwise. School buses and trucks are limited to 65 mph (55 mph on freeways posted below 70).

source.quote: 70 mph maximum/55 mph minimum – On all freeways unless posted otherwise.

facts.value: 55 mph freeway minimum; slow traffic keeps right
facts.detail: Freeways have a 55 mph minimum unless posted otherwise. On a freeway with three or more lanes, drivers at or near the minimum speed should stay in the lane with slower traffic.

source.quote: On a freeway with three or more lanes of travel in the same direction, you may drive in any lane. However, if driving at or near the minimum speed limit, stay in the lane with the slower moving traffic.

facts.value: Allowed after a full stop unless a sign prohibits it
facts.detail: After stopping at the stop line or crosswalk, you may turn right on red unless a sign or signal prohibits it. You must yield to pedestrians, bicyclists and other traffic.

source.quote: may make a right turn from a 1-way or 2-way street into a 2-way street or into a 1-way street carrying traffic in the direction of the right turn or may make a left turn from a 1-way or 2-way street into a 1-way roadway carrying traffic in the direction of the left turn, unless prohibited by sign, signal, marking, light, or other traffic control device.

facts.value: Allowed onto a one-way street (from a one-way or two-way street) after a full stop
facts.detail: Michigan allows a left turn on red onto a one-way street carrying traffic to the left, from either a one-way or a two-way street, after a complete stop and yielding, unless prohibited by sign.

source.quote: When turning left from a two-way street onto a one-way street at a red light, you must come to a full stop, scan for vehicles approaching from the right, and yield the right of way to any vehicles opposite you that are turning right at the intersection.

facts.value: Pull to the right edge and stop; stay 500 feet behind
facts.detail: When an emergency vehicle approaches with lights and siren, pull to the edge of the road clear of intersections and stop until it passes. Stay at least 500 feet behind a moving emergency vehicle using lights and siren, and never pass one unless directed.

source.quote: Stay at least 500 feet behind any moving emergency vehicle displaying flashing warning lights and sounding a siren.

facts.value: Slow at least 10 mph below the limit and move over a lane
facts.detail: For a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights, slow to at least 10 mph below the posted limit and move over a lane if traffic and conditions allow; if you can't move over, slow down and keep as much space as possible.

source.quote: The law requires you to slow down at least 10 mph below the posted speed limit and move over a lane if traffic and conditions allow.

facts.value: Stop at least 20 feet away; not required across a barrier-divided highway
facts.detail: Stop at least 20 feet from a school bus with red overhead lights flashing and stay stopped until the lights go off or the bus moves. Traffic on the other side of a highway divided by a barrier (concrete or grass median, island) need not stop. Fines are doubled.

source.quote: Stop at least 20 feet from a school bus with its red overhead lights flashing; it is picking up or dropping off passengers. It is not necessary to stop for a school bus stopped on the other side of a highway divided by a barrier such as a concrete or grass median, island or other structures that separate the flow of traffic.

facts.value: 3 to 4 seconds (up to 6+ in poor conditions)
facts.detail: Keep a 3- to 4-second following distance. Increase it up to 6 seconds or more at higher speeds or in adverse conditions. Leave at least 3 or 4 seconds behind motorcycles, scooters and bicycles.

source.quote: A 3- to 4-second following distance is required.

facts.value: Half hour after sunset to half hour before sunrise, and when you can't see 500 feet
facts.detail: Headlights must be on from one half-hour after sunset until one half-hour before sunrise, and any time you cannot clearly see people and vehicles 500 feet ahead. Using only parking lights is illegal when headlights are required.

source.quote: Headlights must be turned on one half-hour after sunset until one half-hour before sunrise and at other times when visibility is reduced.

facts.value: Within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle
facts.detail: It is illegal to use or even flash high beams within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle. Dim your lights for pedestrians and cyclists too.

source.quote: It is illegal to use or even flash high-beam headlights within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle.

facts.value: Do not use high beams behind other vehicles (no distance stated)
facts.detail: The handbook says not to use high beams when behind other vehicles because the glare in their mirrors is distracting, but it gives no specific distance.

source.quote: Do not use high beams when behind other vehicles.

facts.value: 15 feet
facts.detail: Never park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant.

source.quote: Within 15 feet of a fire hydrant.

facts.value: 20 feet
facts.detail: Never park within 20 feet of a marked crosswalk, or within a crosswalk.

source.quote: Within 20 feet of a marked crosswalk or 15 feet of an intersection if there is no crosswalk.

facts.value: 15 feet (if no crosswalk)
facts.detail: Never park within 15 feet of an intersection if there is no crosswalk, or within an intersection.

source.quote: Within 20 feet of a marked crosswalk or 15 feet of an intersection if there is no crosswalk.

facts.value: 30 feet
facts.detail: Never park within 30 feet of a stop sign, traffic light or flashing beacon, including a warning sign.

source.quote: Within 30 feet of a stop sign, traffic light or flashing beacon, including a warning sign.

facts.value: 50 feet
facts.detail: Never park within 50 feet of the nearest rail of a railroad crossing.

source.quote: Within 50 feet of the nearest rail of a railroad crossing.

facts.value: 20 feet (same side); 75 feet across the street when marked
facts.detail: Never park within 20 feet of a fire station driveway on the same side of the street, or within 75 feet of it on the other side when marked.

source.quote: Within 20 feet of a fire station driveway on the same side of the street or, when marked, within 75 feet of the driveway on the other side of the street.

facts.value: No more than 12 inches from the curb
facts.detail: Never park more than 12 inches (one foot) from the curb. The parallel-parking steps say not to park more than 6-12 inches from the curb.

source.quote: More than 12 inches from the curb. This means the curb should never be more than a foot from your parked vehicle.

facts.value: Between 15 and 50 feet from the tracks
facts.detail: If a train is coming, stop no more than 50 feet and no less than 15 feet from the tracks. If a stop sign is posted at the crossing, stop whether or not a train is in sight.

source.quote: If a train is coming, all vehicles must stop no more than 50 feet or less than 15 feet from the tracks.

facts.value: At least 3 feet
facts.detail: Leave at least 3 feet between your vehicle and a bicyclist when passing; if that is impractical, pass at a safe distance and speed. You may pass a bicyclist in a no-passing zone when it is safe. Some cities require 5 feet.

source.quote: Michigan law requires that you leave at least 3 feet of space between your vehicle and a bicyclist when passing.

facts.value: Yield to pedestrians in marked or unmarked crosswalks, even on a green light
facts.detail: Drivers must yield to pedestrians in a marked crosswalk (at an intersection or midblock), in a crosswalk even when the driver's light is green, when turning, and to people with a white cane or guide dog.

source.quote: To a pedestrian in the crosswalk, even if your traffic light is green.

facts.value: Notify police if anyone is injured or damage exceeds $1,000
facts.detail: Do not leave the scene. Move drivable vehicles out of the main roadway if there is no serious injury or death and it is safe, exchange information, and notify police if there are injuries or property damage exceeding $1,000.

source.quote: Notify the police if there are injuries or property damage exceeding $1,000.

facts.value: $250,000/$500,000 bodily injury by default (may choose $50,000/$100,000); $10,000 property damage
facts.detail: Since July 2, 2020, the default bodily injury liability limits are $250,000 per person and $500,000 per accident; policyholders may choose lower limits, but not below $50,000 per person and $100,000 per accident. The required property damage liability limit (for accidents in another state) is $10,000.

source.quote: may choose to purchase lower limits than required under subsection (1)(a) and (b), but not lower than $50,000.00 under subsection (1)(a) and $100,000.00 under subsection (1)(b).

facts.value: 12 points in 2 years (or 6 one-point violations) triggers a reexamination
facts.detail: Points stay on your record for two years from the conviction date. Six or more one-point violations, or 12 or more points within two years, require a driver assessment reexamination. Examples: 6 points for OWI or refusing a chemical test; 4 points for 16+ mph over; 3 points for 11-15 over; 2 points for 6-10 over.

source.quote: If you have six or more one-point violations, or 12 or more points on your driving record within a two-year

facts.value: Required unless 21+ with 2 years' endorsement or a safety course, plus $20,000 medical coverage
facts.detail: Motorcycle operators and riders must wear helmets. A rider 21 or older may ride without one only if they have had a motorcycle endorsement for at least 2 years or passed an approved safety course, and carry at least $20,000 in first-party medical benefits.

source.quote: A person who is operating a motorcycle is not required to wear a crash helmet on his or her head if he or she has had a motorcycle endorsement on his or her operator's or chauffeur's license for not less than 2 years or the person passes a motorcycle safety course conducted under section 811a or 811b and satisfies the requirements of subdivision (c).

facts.value: Illegal
facts.detail: Motorcyclists and moped riders may not pass between lines of traffic. Motorcycles are entitled to full use of a lane and may ride no more than 2 abreast.

source.quote: A person operating a motorcycle, moped, low-speed vehicle, electric personal assistive mobility device, or electric skateboard shall not pass between lines of traffic

notableLaws.title: Michigan Lefts (indirect left turns)
notableLaws.summary: At intersections with Michigan Lefts, direct left turns are not allowed. To turn left, drive straight through the intersection (or turn right), then make a U-turn at a median crossover. An unmarked crossover is a single-lane crossover.

source.quote: Intersections that have Michigan Lefts do not allow traditional left-turn movements. Instead, to turn left, a person must drive straight through the intersection, or turn right, then make a U-turn at a median crossover.

notableLaws.title: Work zones: 45 mph, double fines and extra points
notableLaws.summary: Most construction, maintenance or surveying work zones have a 45 mph limit unless posted otherwise. Fines are doubled for moving violations, and speeding there adds extra points: 3 points for 10 mph or less over, 4 for more than 10 up to 15, and 5 for more than 15.

source.quote: Fines are doubled for all moving violations in work zones. In addition, motorists caught speeding in construction zones face increased points on their driving records.

notableLaws.title: Flashing green lights on road maintenance vehicles
notableLaws.summary: State and local road agencies may add flashing or oscillating green lights to maintenance vehicles, used only while road work is under way. When you see them, slow down and drive with caution. Private contractors may not use green lights.

source.quote: Motorists should know that when they see flashing green lights on a local or state maintenance vehicle to slow down and drive with caution.

notableLaws.title: Funeral processions have the right of way
notableLaws.summary: Funeral processions have the right of way over all vehicles except fire trucks, ambulances and police vehicles. Cutting through a procession is a civil infraction, but drivers do not have to pull over.

source.quote: Funeral processions have the right of way over all other vehicles, except for fire trucks, ambulances and police vehicles.

notableLaws.title: Keep right on interstates and freeways
notableLaws.summary: On an interstate or full-access-controlled freeway you must drive in the right-hand lane, except for congestion, weather, a hazard in the right lane, yielding to emergency/construction vehicles, or when no traffic is immediately ahead of or behind you in the left lane.

source.quote: When driving on an interstate highway or full-access controlled freeway, you must drive in the right-hand lane.

notableLaws.title: Horses and buggies: slow to 15-20 mph and keep 20 feet back
notableLaws.summary: When following a horse and rider or horse-drawn buggy, slow to 15-20 mph and stay at least 20 feet back. Never honk or rev the engine. Slow-moving vehicles (25 mph or less) display an orange triangle.

source.quote: When following a horse and rider or a horse-drawn buggy, reduce your speed to 15-20 mph and maintain a safe distance of at least 20 feet between your vehicle and the rider or buggy so as not to spook the horse.

notableLaws.title: Deer crashes: don't veer
notableLaws.summary: About 60,000 vehicle-deer crashes happen in Michigan each year. If a crash is unavoidable, do not swerve: stay in your lane, brake firmly, hold the wheel with both hands and come to a controlled stop. Report a deer crash to law enforcement or the DNR.

source.quote: Do not veer for deer; stay in your lane.

notableLaws.title: Move drivable vehicles after a minor crash
notableLaws.summary: If a crash causes no serious injury or death, a driver or passenger with a valid license must move a drivable vehicle out of the main roadway (to the shoulder, median or a nearby lot) when it is safe.

source.quote: Vehicles involved in crashes that do not result in serious injury or death shall be moved from the main roadway by the driver or a passenger with a valid driver's license if the vehicle can be driven and it is safe to do so.

notableLaws.title: No riders under 18 in an open pickup bed over 15 mph
notableLaws.summary: Anyone under 18 may not ride in the open bed of a pickup traveling more than 15 mph, with exceptions for farm, construction, military, parade and emergency uses.

source.quote: Anyone under 18 years old is prohibited from riding in the open bed of a pickup truck traveling more than 15 mph.

notableLaws.title: Children under 6 may not be left unattended in a vehicle
notableLaws.summary: It is illegal to leave a child younger than 6 unattended in a vehicle when the time or circumstances pose an unreasonable risk of harm; leaving them with someone 13 or older who is not legally incapacitated is allowed.

source.quote: Under Michigan law, it is illegal to leave children younger than 6 years old unattended in a vehicle if the amount of time or circumstances in which they are left poses an unreasonable risk of harm or injury.

notableLaws.title: First OWI conviction: 180-day license suspension
notableLaws.summary: For a first conviction of operating while intoxicated (no prior convictions within 7 years), the Secretary of State suspends the license for 180 days, and no restricted license may be issued during the first 30 days.

source.quote: For 180 days for a violation of section 625(1) or (8) before October 31, 2010 or, beginning October 31, 2010, section 625(1)(a) or (b) or (8) if the individual has no prior convictions within 7 years. The secretary of state may issue the individual a restricted license during a specified portion of the suspension, except that the secretary of state shall not issue a restricted license during the first 30 days of suspension.

notableLaws.title: New drivers are on probation for at least 3 years
notableLaws.summary: All newly licensed drivers, including GDL teens, are placed on probation for a minimum of three years; probationary and GDL drivers may be called to a driver reexamination after only one or two violations.

source.quote: New drivers, including teen drivers under Graduated Driver Licensing, are placed on probation for a minimum of three years.

gaps: signal_distance: neither the handbook nor MCL 257.648 states a minimum distance for signaling before a turn or lane change; the handbook only says to always use your turn signal.
high_beam_dim_following: the handbook says not to use high beams behind other vehicles but gives no distance; MCL 257.700 sets only the 500-foot rule for oncoming vehicles.

bac_limit_adult / bac_limit_under21 / bac_limit_commercial / implied_consent / open_container: the handbook does not state BAC numbers, the refusal suspension length or the open-container rule, so these come from the Michigan Vehicle Code (MCL 257.625, 625m, 625f, 624a). MCL 257.625 provides that the 0.08 limit rises to 0.10 five years after a state treasurer certification under subsection (28); no such change is in effect, so 0.08 is recorded.
speed_limit_school_zone: the handbook only says school-zone limits vary and are posted; the 25 mph floor / 20 mph maximum reduction comes from MCL 257.627a.
speed_limit_business_district: the handbook says to watch for posted limits in business districts; the 25 mph default is from MCL 257.627(2)(b).
insurance_minimums: not in the handbook; taken from MCL 500.3009 (also summarized by DIFS at michigan.gov/autoinsurance). Personal injury protection (PIP) choices are not recorded.
motorcycle_helmet_law / motorcycle_lane_splitting: not in the car handbook; taken from MCL 257.658 and 257.660. The Michigan Motorcycle Operator Manual (SOS-116) was not reviewed.
motorcycleTest: the Secretary of State motorcycle pages describe the motorcycle knowledge test but do not publish its number of questions or passing score.

knowledgeTest.questions/passingScore: the Secretary of State does not publish the number of questions or passing score for the adult operator knowledge test; the recorded 80 questions / 70% is the teen Segment 1 state exam from the MDOS Driver Education Curriculum Guide (Section 6, 03/2022).
officialPracticeTests: the only official sample test found is the 10-question Safe Driving Knowledge Test inside the handbook (pp. 83-84); its standalone PDF link on michigan.gov returned 404.
